paragraphs.text: Among the prized possessions of most churches in Naples are elaborate Baroque Nativity scenes, made of wood, terra-cotta, wax, and delicate fabrics. To this day, there is a whole street devoted to the construction of these detailed set pieces, which, in addition to the Nativity, depict everyday life—fruit sellers, animals, shepherds—in rich detail. The Met owns a large collection, which it displays in a lively tableau at the foot of a giant Christmas tree in the Medieval Sculpture Hall. (Metropolitan Museum of Art; through Jan. 6.)

Last year, the centenary of the Rockettes was celebrated with a new sound system rather than a new number, but this year that oversight is being corrected. The choreographer Chloé Arnold (“Spirited,” “The Late Late Show with James Corden”) has been hired to sharpen a sometimes neglected aspect of the Rockettes’ tradition: their tap dancing. Her intricate, girl-power routine to a remixed “Carol of the Bells” joins old favorites like “Parade of the Wooden Soldiers,” made in 1933 and built to last. (Radio City Music Hall; through Jan. 4.)

Matthew Warchus’s immersive staging of Charles Dickens’s Yuletide classic returns to PAC NYC, albeit with a twist. The crotchety skinflint Ebenezer Scrooge is being played by Andy Karl, cast boldly against type. Karl’s virile charisma energized the lead roles in musicalizations of “Rocky” and “Groundhog Day.” Will a shirtless Scrooge take swings at those pesky charity collectors? Either way, viewers should expect carolling, a complimentary clementine or gingerbread cookie, and, despite Scrooge’s best efforts, Christmas cheer. (PAC NYC; through Jan. 3.)

If the thought of another “Christmas Carol” triggers your inner Scrooge, this riff may excite your chilly little heart. Kevin Zak’s unorthodox adaptation camps up the chestnut: on Oscars Eve, Cate Blanchett (Josh Sharp), rich in accolades, is visited by three spirits of Nicole Kidman (Marla Mindelle, fresh off “Titaníque”). They take her on a journey through the Australian outback and a Dickensian Tinsel Town to impart the true meaning of awards season. (New World Stages; through Dec. 30.)

“The Nutcracker” pops up all over town, from Bushwick’s “Nutcracker Rouge” (Théâtre XIV; Dec. 10-13)—a naughty romp that reinvents the Kingdom of the Sweets as a carnal coming-of-age story, replete with trapeze acts and stiletto-heeled burlesque—to Flatbush, where the Kings Theatre brings back “The Hip Hop Nutcracker” (Dec. 23), in which the dances are a reflection of the city’s street life. “The Yorkville Nutcracker,” a cozy production by the late Francis Patrelle, turns thirty this year; the starry guest dancers Miriam Miller and Tyler Angle perform as Sugarplum and her Cavalier. (Kaye Playhouse; Dec. 10-13.) The mother of all “Nutcrackers” is still George Balanchine’s familiar and sumptuous production for New York City Ballet, with its giant tree, heart-in-the-throat snow scene, and windswept Dewdrop solo—a rush of pure movement amid the waltzing flowers. (David H. Koch Theatre; Nov. 27-Jan. 2.)

In what has become a cherished annual tradition, the indie-rock band Yo La Tengo returns for a series of Hanukkah shows. Across the holiday’s eight nights, a surprise musician or comedian opens the show, the hosts are joined by guests, and every evening ends with an encore of covers. Past guests have included Lucinda Williams, Fred Armisen, the Sun Ra Arkestra, and Lucy Dacus. As if that wasn’t enough of an enticement, all of the proceeds go to various charities. (Bowery Ballroom; Dec. 4-11.)

Sergei Prokofiev’s “symphonic tale for children” has a dual purpose: to tell an engaging story about a young boy who pulls himself out of a pickle, and to introduce the instruments of the orchestra. Each character—boy, wolf, cat, bird—is associated with a particular instrument. This version, a holiday fixture performed in the little theatre beneath the Guggenheim Museum since 2013, moves the action to Central Park; Isaac Mizrahi narrates with wry humor, the dancers of Dance Heginbotham embody the different characters, and Ensemble Connect plays Prokofiev’s score. (Guggenheim Museum; Dec. 5-13.)

It’s no secret that the city has a special glimmer during the holiday season—it almost feels like angelic voices are serenading you as you walk down the street. In fact, you might not be imagining them. This winter season, there will be festive chanting by the Grace Chorale of Brooklyn (Dec. 19-20), readings and carols by the Dessoff Choirs (Dec. 5), folk songs by the Vienna Boys’ Choir (Dec. 20), candlelight tunes by Voices of Ascension (Dec. 9, 10, 14, and 15), and holiday songs from Cher and Mariah Carey by the New York City Gay Men’s Chorus, in “Yuletide Gay(er)” (Dec. 11-12).

Hark, is that the herald angels singing? Oh, wait, no, that’s just every choral group in New York—it’s “Messiah” season! The Oratorio Society will perform it for the hundred-and-fifty-second consecutive time, at Carnegie Hall (Dec. 21), while the New York Classical Players will bring it alive for their first, across the city and in New Jersey (Dec. 4-6). The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra performs at St. Ann’s Church, featuring the New York Choral Society (Dec. 20)—in Brooklyn, obviously. The New York Philharmonic might take the cake, though—their performance includes one of the most aptly named soloists of the season, the countertenor John Holiday (Dec. 10-13). As Handel said, “Hallelujah!”
